entry.title: The cached card_ids list is copied before it is popped from
entry.content:
The cached card_ids list is copied before it is popped from

`get_across_target_notes` caches a query's card ids in extra_state, then the
select_card_by="None" branch pops from that same list object. The cache and the
working list were one list, so selecting cards edited the cached entry: a later
call reusing it would get the query's result with the already-selected cards
missing from it, silently.

Both sides now hold their own list.

Latent today rather than observed - the branch needs select_card_count > 0, and
the three Across notes definitions measured in the note-adding phase all use 0,
which takes the "all cards" path above it instead. It stops being latent the
moment extra_state is threaded across notes the way file_cache beside it already
is, which is the only thing that would make this cache worth having.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

entry.title: The selected-card cache is stored, not assigned over
entry.content:
The selected-card cache is stored, not assigned over

`get_across_target_notes` cached its Least_reps pick with

    extra_state = {card_select_key: selected_card_id}

which rebinds the local name rather than storing into the caller's dict. Two
things followed: the entry never reached the caller, and everything already in
the dict was discarded - including the `card_ids` this same call cached a few
lines earlier, which is the expensive half.

Found while measuring the note-adding phase of a match_words_to_notes run, where
copy_on_add definitions are 71% of the clock. This is not that cost: the branch
is only reached when select_card_by is "Least_reps", and the three Across notes
definitions in that profile all use "None". A correctness fix, worth ~0 there.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

entry.title: related_card_disperse: bury across all decks, not just one tree
entry.content:
related_card_disperse: bury across all decks, not just one tree

The deck browser's "Disperse due cards" gathered its session from
deck_and_child_ids(deck_id) and then discarded every related card
outside it, even though rule queries are not deck-scoped. On the live
collection this meant the command could report "No two related cards
were going to come up together" on a session with dozens of real
collisions, because they all pointed from one top-level deck tree into
another.

Also fixes, found alongside the root cause:
- only queue=2 (review) was gathered; interday and intraday learning
  cards due today were invisible to a normal-deck run
- a nested filtered deck's row-number `due` was sorted against its
  siblings' real due dates
- a rule whose code raises was indistinguishable from a rule that
  found nothing, on both the deck run and the sync path (live: a rule
  starting with `import re` has been failing on every run since
  `__import__` isn't in the sandboxed builtins)
- the daily limit excluded learning cards from the cap while including
  them in the session, undercounting the limit

The session is now the union of every deck's own session today, as
per-deck blocks concatenated rather than one global sort: the deck the
run was started on leads (so a cross-deck collision buries the *other*
deck's card), the rest follow in name order. Cross-deck burying is
on by default (matching the review hook's existing behavior) with a
new "Disperse due cards across all decks" option to opt back into the
single-deck scope.

Buried-deck attribution and rule-error summaries are now shown in the
tooltip so both failure modes are visible instead of silent.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Sonnet 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

entry.title: Fix query input stretching the dialog horizontally
entry.content:
Fix query input stretching the dialog horizontally

Two causes. The description label in InterpolatedTextEditLayout was
missing setWordWrap(True), unlike its counterpart in CodeEditLayout.
Without word wrap, QLabel's minimumSizeHint equals the full text width,
so the layout was forced to at least that width whenever query_text_widget
became visible -- which is exactly when a non-code-mode rule is selected.

The AutoResizingTextEdit also lacked an explicit WidgetWidth line wrap
mode and a horizontal scroll bar policy of AlwaysOff. Without those, the
document's unconstrained ideal width could propagate through sizeHint and
push the layout wider, and long queries required horizontal scrolling
within the input instead of wrapping and growing taller.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Sonnet 4.6 <noreply@anthropic.com>

entry.title: Add "Disperse siblings for all note types"
entry.content:
Add "Disperse siblings for all note types"

The replacement for custom_schedule_helper's old auto-disperse siblings
setting. On, every note type that makes more than one card per note --
more than one template, or a cloze note type whatever its template count
-- and that no stored rule names disperses the reviewed note's own cards,
on review and on sync alike.

Those rules are worked out from the note type in hand at the point a rule
would run, not materialised for the collection: a reviewed card only ever
needs its own note type's default, and rules_for_model keeps the cost to
a set lookup. Their guids carry a prefix, because runs are deduped and
grouped by guid and a derived rule needs one that is stable across calls
but cannot collide with a stored rule's uuid.

The dialog lists them greyed out and italic after the stored rules. They
stay derived while they are only being read -- a commit compares the form
against the baseline before it promotes anything -- so clicking through
them changes nothing. The first real edit promotes one in place with a
uuid of its own, which is how a note type gets a query of its own or,
saved with dispersal off, opts out of the default entirely.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

entry.title: Drop disperse siblings from custom_schedule_helper
entry.content:
Drop disperse siblings from custom_schedule_helper

The related_card_disperse addon now covers this, and does more: it
disperses by note and by configurable relations between notes, and
registers both the reviewer_did_answer_card and sync_did_finish hooks
that this code used to own.

Removing the review-time hook left schedule/__init__.py empty, and
removing the after-sync one left sync_hook's `texts` accumulator dead --
it existed only to funnel the reschedule message into the disperse
tooltip, and reschedule already tooltips its own result.

The 'd' custom data marker stays live in reschedule's filter, since
related_card_disperse writes the same one, so auto reschedule must still
skip those cards.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

entry.title: Add "Disperse due cards": bury a session's colliding cards
entry.content:
Add "Disperse due cards": bury a session's colliding cards

Rescheduling disperses the future; it cannot disperse a backlog, because
a backlogged card's due date no longer decides anything but whether the
card joins today's pool. Burying works on the pool itself. It is
unaffected by the review order, survives moving cards between decks and
rebuilding filtered decks, changes no scheduling data, and Anki lifts it
at the day rollover on its own.

The new item on the deck list's gear menu reads the session the deck will
actually deal out, finds the rule relations within it, walks it in order
keeping the first card of each collision, and buries the rest in a single
bury_cards call -- one undo step, buried as the scheduler rather than as
the user, since this is the job Anki's own sibling burying does. Running
it again finds nothing: a buried card leaves the session, and what
remains has no two related cards in it.

A filtered deck needs no modelling. Filling one rewrites each card's due
with its row number in the deck's own search order and parks the real
date in odue, and a filtered deck has no preset, so the queue builder
falls back to ordering reviews by due -- which is that row number. For a
normal deck the preset's review order is reproduced clause for clause
from rslib's review_order_sql, down to the fnvhash tiebreak, and the list
is cut at the deck tree's review count.

New bury_min_gap setting: 0, shown as "whole session", means one card per
group per day like Anki's sibling burying. A larger value only buries a
card when a related one sits within that many kept cards -- kept, because
a buried card is never shown and so cannot space anything out.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

entry.title: Report pinned backlog rather than an empty updated count
entry.content:
Report pinned backlog rather than an empty updated count

A rule run over a backlogged group would otherwise report a large
candidate count, updated=0, and "due ranges too tight to separate" --
each true, and together misleading about why nothing happened. Outcome
lines now carry backlogged=N when it bit, a fully pinned group says so
by name, and a run whose cards all turned out to be already in place no
longer claims to have dispersed them.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

entry.title: Pin backlogged cards instead of rescheduling them
entry.content:
Pin backlogged cards instead of rescheduling them

Anki gathers every card with due <= today into one pool and hands the
deck's review order straight to the SQL that orders it, then lets the
daily limit truncate that stream. Under any order that is not a due-date
one -- ascending retrievability, say, which reads the card's last review
time out of its FSRS data and ignores due and ivl entirely -- a
backlogged card's due date decides only whether it joins the pool. Where
in the past the date sits changes nothing about when the card comes up,
and moving it into the future postpones a card that is already late.

So a backlogged card in such a deck is now pinned at its current date. It
still anchors its group, and the cards that can still be moved arrange
themselves around it. Decks that do order by due date are untouched:
there the date really does drive both the order and the truncation, and
dispersing a backlog across it works as intended.

The deck consulted is the card's home deck, not the one it is sitting in:
a card in a filtered deck is shown in that deck's build order and takes
its real due date back with it when it leaves.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

entry.title: Stop a dispersal from stamping unmoved cards onto tomorrow
entry.content:
Stop a dispersal from stamping unmoved cards onto tomorrow

apply_disperse_plan floored every card in the plan at today + 1,
including the ones the optimiser had deliberately left alone. For a card
that is already overdue, "leave it where it was" therefore became "make
it due tomorrow": a run over a backlogged deck moved almost every card
in it onto a single day, which is neither dispersal nor a no-op.

The skip has to be per card rather than per plan, because a group
normally mixes movable cards with pinned ones, and _is_noop_plan only
catches the case where nothing at all moved.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

entry.title: Add per-trigger controls for the review tooltip
entry.content:
Add per-trigger controls for the review tooltip

Three new global settings gate what the review hook shows:
- "Don't show report during review" suppresses the tooltip entirely;
  when enabled the other two options are disabled in the dialog.
- "Don't show details in report during review" collapses the per-rule
  messages into a single summary line (same as the browser tooltip).
- "Don't show report on runs that rescheduled nothing during review"
  suppresses the tooltip for outcomes where nothing moved.

The old show_unchanged_outcome flag (True = show unchanged) is migrated
on load to hide_review_unchanged (inverted). Browser and sync tooltips
are unaffected: the browser always shows the summary-only tooltip, and
the sync path always reports all outcomes.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Sonnet 4.6 <noreply@anthropic.com>

entry.title: Disperse a browser selection without reviewing it
entry.content:
Disperse a browser selection without reviewing it

Reviews done on a phone never run the review hook, and a rule added after
the fact has never run at all; either way the next session still holds the
cards those rules would have moved. Right-clicking a browser selection now
runs the dispersal over it directly.

In notes mode a rule that applies to a whole note runs once per note where
it can: the run reports the raw ids its query returned, and every card of
the note among them is taken off the queue, with the remainder anchoring
another run until none are left. The anchor is dropped whether or not the
query returned it, so a query gated to a card type the anchor is not cannot
loop forever on the same card.

A rule that names card types instead runs per card of those types. Pointing
two card types of one note at the same group is user error, but it is the
config saying so, not something to optimise away.

Cards mode gets no such grouping: the selection already names the cards the
user meant, so each anchors its own runs.

Rules are matched on note and card type only. The on-review and on-sync
flags say which automatic trigger a rule wants, and an explicit run from the
browser is neither of them.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

entry.title: Let a rule target card types, not just note types
entry.content:
Let a rule target card types, not just note types

Dispersal logic was defined per note type, on the assumption that every card of
a note relates to the same other cards. That breaks down when one card type
shows only some of the note's fields: cards that never reveal the rest are not
spoiling anything for the notes related through those fields, and should not be
dispersed against them.

Rules gain target_card_types, a list of "NoteType<::>Card type" names alongside
the note type targets. Empty -- what every existing rule migrates to -- means
every card type, so behaviour is unchanged until a rule says otherwise. The
targets are a gate on whether the rule runs at all: a card outside them never
reaches the query. Two rules on one note type with different card types is how
one note type gets two different queries. Cloze notes resolve to their single
template name; ordinals of one template show the same fields, so telling them
apart would not buy anything.

Queries also gain __Reviewed_Card_Template and __Reviewed_Card_Ord, handed to
interpolation as variables since a note-level {{Field}} cannot see which card
was reviewed. The ord is exposed 1-based so it drops straight into a card:N
search term.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

entry.title: Move the rule buttons into the footer, outside the scroll area
entry.content:
Move the rule buttons into the footer, outside the scroll area

A rule with a long query scrolls the editor, and the buttons that act on the
rule went with it: saving meant scrolling back down to find Save rule. Move up,
Move down, New rule, Save rule and Delete rule now sit in the footer next to
Save and Cancel, which never scrolls. The validation message follows them, so
the reason Save is disabled stays visible alongside the disabled button.

entry.title: Inset the dialog from the screen edge so it stays resizable
entry.content:
Inset the dialog from the screen edge so it stays resizable

resize() sizes the client area, so opening at the exact available width pushed
the window frame -- and the resize handles with it -- a few pixels off both
sides of the screen, leaving the dialog impossible to resize horizontally.
Inset it by the frame's worth on each side.
